quote: If I recall correctly, an average individual has two to ten somatically expressed mutations.
content: The mutation count was wrong, and "If I recall correctly" was warranted. The argument rests on the next sentence: "any given aspect of someone's disposition is probably not very far from average." That is the polygenic point Fable makes. Traits are roughly normal, most people sit near the mean, and a trait extreme enough to produce unprovoked machine-kicking sits in a thin tail. "Mutant" is the essay's word for that tail. The prior comparison is between a common situation (late buses) and an uncommon disposition (the tail), and Fable's own figures support it: two standard deviations above the mean is about 2% of the population, which is a prior worth shouldering reluctantly.

quote: The “fundamental attribution error” refers to our tendency to overattribute others’ behaviors to their dispositions, while reversing this tendency for ourselves.
content: Malle's meta-analysis found the actor–observer asymmetry only for negative events, and the essay's example is a negative event: kicking a vending machine that has eaten your lunch money. The surviving part of the effect covers the case the essay uses (Malle 2006). The essay's subject is the correspondence bias in the observer. Its title, its Gilbert & Malone epigraph and its Jones & Harris evidence all concern that, and Fable calls it robust. The sentence Fable quotes is the textbook definition of the "fundamental attribution error" as textbooks gave it in 2007. The essay's argument depends on the observer half, which is intact.

quote: Yes, people do have dispositions—but there are not enough heritable quirks of disposition to directly account for all the surface behaviors you see.
content: Fleeson's result supports the essay. Each person's behaviour varies so widely across situations that one act is weak evidence about the stable mean of their distribution (Fleeson 2001). Traits correlating about .3 with a single behaviour, as Funder & Ozer found, means roughly 90% of the variance in that act is left over. So an observer who reads a trait off one kick is overshooting, which is the correspondence bias. The essay grants dispositions ("Yes, people do have dispositions"). What it denies is that single surface behaviours "directly" map onto heritable quirks. On that point the draw Fable describes is its best evidence.

quote: Perhaps I am a victim of false consensus; perhaps I overestimate how many people would press the green button if they saw the situation in those terms. But y’know, I’d still bet there’d be at least a substantial minority.
content: Dawes shows that using your own response as one data point about others is Bayesian-correct, which makes the essay's bet ("at least a substantial minority") the modest, legitimate use of false consensus. Krueger and Clement found a residual "truly false" consensus beyond the Bayesian amount (Krueger & Clement 1994), and the essay concedes that residual in so many words. The subordinate clause is not dropped, either. It is the essay's thesis applied to its author: unusual beliefs call for explanation, and the actions those beliefs imply do not. "If you see the situation in those terms" is stated outright, so the two buttons illustrate the conditional without presupposing its antecedent.
